name: Sam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a framing carpenter for Rob Hendry, a builder in the market town where I grew up. We do barn conversions, new houses in the villages, the odd farm shed. This month we're turning an old stone barn at Ashby Farm into a family house, so I'm putting in the new roof structure and floors inside the old walls. Seven of us on the books, and Rob's on site every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can drive past half the houses round here and say I built that roof. What wears me out is the mud on farm sites in winter, and old barns where nothing is straight. My girlfriend Ana's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and my dad's a bricklayer, so it's a working family. I use an AI app now and then to check timber sizes, once the other lads showed me it was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never thought it was going to build a roof anyway. I'd say it at football on Sunday and probably get a laugh. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays steady and I can get on with my life. Barns still need converting, villages still need houses. A barn that's stood crooked for two hundred years needs a carpenter who can see it, not a computer. My worry is just house prices, because Ana and I want to buy and it's hard on two normal wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Rob and keep saving for a deposit with Ana, about three hundred a month between us. I'd keep using the timber app when it's handy. I'd probably do the extra overtime on Saturdays in spring to speed up the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's an ordinary life, and ordinary is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan with Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been together four years. I'm going to ask her to marry me next year, she doesn't know yet. After that, a house in the town, and kids when we can afford them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about Rob's firm change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Rob might use one of those apps for his quotes, he's been grumbling about evenings spent on paperwork. On site it'd be exactly the same.

say: He **never expected** AI to build a roof anyway.
He'd joke about it at **Sunday football** but not post online.
think: Barns and villages still need **carpenters** who can see crooked old structures.
His real worry is **house prices** on two ordinary wages.
do: Keep working for **Rob Hendry** on barn conversions and village houses.
Save **three hundred a month** with his girlfriend for a deposit.
Work **Saturday overtime** in spring to speed up the deposit.
feel: **Calm**, wanting an **ordinary life** to carry on.
S0.quote: A barn that's stood crooked for two hundred years needs a carpenter who can see it, not a computer.
fieldNote: His life plans are clear: **proposal, house, children**.
He uses AI only **once it's proven** by workmates.
Worry centres on **affording a home**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep framing roofs on Rob Hendry's barn conversions
Work Saturday overtime in spring towards the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hands-on trades come out of this better than most. I'd tell the younger lads to stay on the tools and learn properly. I'd probably say it at church too, because a few of the parents there work in offices and they'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own job's fine for a good while. But Ana's work, the marking and the reports and the reading help, that's the kind of thing they'd try software on. My job is safe for years, but I'm not sure the school will keep paying for a teaching assistant. Rob's office lady, Pat, does all the orders and invoices, and she'd be worried too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever estimating app Rob brings in, once he's tried it on a couple of jobs. I'd keep saving and maybe push to four hundred a month in case Ana's hours get cut. I'd still propose next year, I'm not changing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Ana. My side feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Ana's hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage on my wage for a while, it's tight but doable. Her mum's offered help before and we've always said no. We'd probably say yes this time, just for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell the younger lads to stay on the tools. Is that what your dad told you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More or less. My dad said get a trade and you'll never go hungry, and he's been right so far. In this picture I think he'd still be right, at least for a while.

say: Hands-on trades come out of this **better than most**.
Younger lads should **stay on the tools** and learn properly.
think: His own job is **safe for years**.
His girlfriend's **teaching assistant** job could be cut back by software.
do: Learn the **estimating app** once his boss has tested it.
Raise deposit saving to **four hundred** a month.
Keep the plan to **propose** next year.
S1.quote: My job is safe for years, but I'm not sure the school will keep paying for a teaching assistant.
fieldNote: His worry runs through the **household**, not his own role.
He'd accept **family help** from her mum, which he'd refused before.
His trust in trades echoes his **father's advice**.

steps.text: Learn Rob's estimating app after Rob tests it on two jobs
Raise deposit saving to four hundred a month
Propose to Ana next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too fast, and I'd say families and churches are going to be holding things together. I'd say it to my dad and to Rob. I'd not go on about it publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot. In 2028 the office jobs go, so people stop buying converted barns and new village houses. Then around 2031 robots that can do hands-on work arrive, and I'm thirty-one. I'd go from saving for a wedding to wondering whether my boss Rob can keep seven men on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the proposal and the house, and keep every penny of the deposit as savings. I'd talk to my dad about the builders he knows, in case Rob runs out of work. Ana and I would look at moving in with her mum for a year to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it might not count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big change, putting off the proposal. How would you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rotten. I've had the ring picked out for months. But I'm not getting married and buying a house in the same year everything falls apart, my dad would say that's daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at retraining, with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, but I wouldn't know what to. Everything I'd retrain into would be hit too, in two years. So I'd stick with what I know and find the firm most likely to survive.

say: It's **too much, too fast** for anyone to cope with.
**Families and churches** will be the ones holding things together.
think: People stop buying **converted barns** when office jobs go in 2028.
Robots reach his **hands-on work** around 2031, when he's thirty-one.
do: Put off the **proposal and house**, keeping the deposit as savings.
Ask his **dad's builder contacts** about work in case the firm struggles.
Move in with his **girlfriend's mum** for a year to save rent.
feel: **Anxious**, feeling he **did everything right** and it might not count.
S2.quote: I'd go from saving for a wedding to wondering whether my boss Rob can keep seven men on.
fieldNote: The fast timeline **upends his life plans**, not just his job.
He relies on **family networks** for both work and housing.
Weighs his **father's judgement** heavily in big decisions.

steps.text: Put off proposing to Ana and buying a house
Keep the deposit money as an emergency cushion
Ask his dad's builder friends about work and stay with Ana's mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, so do it properly. Keep apprentices coming through, keep families together. I'd say it at church and to Rob.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to get ready, but not to relax. AGI around 2031 hits Rob's paperwork and the people who buy his houses, then robots around 2034. Five years means I can still get married, but I'd want a supervisor's ticket before the robots show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose next year as planned but keep the wedding small. I'd do the part-time site supervisor course at the college, two evenings a week for a year, so I can run a site, not just work on one. I'd keep saving four hundred a month and vote for whoever backs apprenticeships and small builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a supervisor course, when supervising has paperwork that AI would take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. But somebody still has to stand on a muddy site and decide what's safe, talk to the farmer and keep the lads in line. That's the bit I'd be learning, more than the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would back it. She's the sensible one, she'd make me a spreadsheet of the savings. She'd probably want a smaller wedding anyway.

say: There's **time** to do this properly, so it should be done properly.
Keep **apprentices** coming through and families together.
think: Five years is **enough to prepare**, but not to relax.
He wants a **supervisor's ticket** before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Propose next year but keep the **wedding small**.
Take a **site supervisor course**, two evenings a week for a year.
Vote for parties backing **apprenticeships and small builders**.
S3.quote: Five years means I can still get married, but I'd want a supervisor's ticket before the robots show up.
fieldNote: He sees the **human side** of supervising as the lasting part.
Accepts a fair challenge **without getting defensive**.
Five years lets him keep **marriage plans** with a smaller wedding.

steps.text: Take the college site supervisor course two evenings a week
Propose to Ana next year and plan a small wedding
Vote for candidates who back apprenticeships and small builders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. I'd say young people should still learn a trade, because ten years of good wages is worth having. I'd say it to my cousins who are leaving school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years suits me fine. I'd be thirty-nine when robots come for hands-on work, around 2039, with a house and probably kids. Ten years of warning is long enough to pay off a good chunk of a mortgage before any robot turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose next year, have a proper wedding, and buy a house in the town within two years. I'd learn the estimating and planning apps properly over time, because by 2036 they'd be doing most of Rob's paperwork. Around year five I'd think about the supervisor course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's far off, but it's still the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids, if you had them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn the computers too. My dad only gave me half of that advice. I'd want my kids to have both halves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's the same ending. Does that change how big a mortgage you'd take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd go smaller than the bank offers. Pay it down hard in the first ten years. My dad always says never owe more than you can pay off while you're still fit.

say: A decade is **plenty of time** for anyone willing to work.
Young people should still **learn a trade** for ten years of wages.
think: He'd be **thirty-nine** with a home and children when robots arrive.
Ten years lets him **pay down a mortgage** before robots turn up.
do: Propose, marry and **buy a house** within two years.
Learn the **estimating and planning** apps properly over time.
Consider the **supervisor course** around year five.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is long enough to pay off a good chunk of a mortgage before any robot turns up.
fieldNote: The decade lets his **family plans** go ahead in full.
He'd give his children **both halves** of the advice: trade and computers.
Shows caution by taking a **smaller mortgage**.

steps.text: Marry Ana and buy a house in the town within two years
Learn the estimating and planning apps Rob uses
Decide on the supervisor course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would mean putting my whole life on hold. What would help is backing for small builders and apprenticeships, so firms like Rob's keep going and keep training people. I don't want a handout, I want my boss Rob's firm still standing in five years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what this does to people my age who want to start a family. Everyone's talking about jobs, but it's also about whether you dare get married and buy a house.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want my boss Rob's firm still standing in five years.
portrait: Sam is a 27-year-old **framing carpenter** on barn conversions and village houses for a small local builder.
He lives with his **teaching-assistant girlfriend** and plans to propose, buy a house and start a family.
He adopts tech **once proven** and leans on his father's judgement.
In a fast scenario he'd put his **life plans** on hold and lean on family.
With more warning, he keeps his **plans** and builds a supervisor's skills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would put his **wedding** and house on hold.
whatWouldHelp: Backing for **small builders** and **apprenticeships** so local firms keep going.
